title: Saemisch against Nimzowitsch, 1923: is it zugzwang?
outcomes: Tries four of the five key moments for Black before seeing the move (the fifth, 24...Bd3, is shown) and compares each attempt with the engine's first choice
Applies the pass test (compare moving with passing) to the final position and says what the engine at depth 16 shows and does not show about it
Says at which point the engine, at depth 16, already rates Black clearly ahead

steps.text: **Saemisch (White) against Nimzowitsch (Black)**, Copenhagen, March 1923 (round 7, 10 March according to chessgames.com and a note in Edward Winter's article). A Queen's Indian Defence. Black won in 25 moves; one account says White ran out of time rather than resigned. Writers disagree whether the finish is a true zugzwang. You play Black at four moments (and read a fifth), then test the last position with the engine.

steps.caption: Moves 1 to 17. Step through them; your first decision comes at the end.

line.say: Both sides develop on the kingside; White's bishop sits on g2.
White plays cxd5 and Black recaptures with the c-pawn.
Black has pieces on c6 and b5; the queenside is where he plays.
The knight goes to h5 and the f-pawn moves to f5.
The queen retreats to d1. Black to move.

claims.statement: 1.d4 is legal.

steps.caption: The game after 17...b4. Step through to White's move 20.

line.say: The pawn attacks the knight on c3.
The knight retreats to b1.
The bishop goes to b5.
The rook goes to g1.
The bishop goes to d6. White to move.

claims.statement: 17...b4 is legal.
At depth 16 the engine does not rate the position as better for White.

steps.caption: White to move on move 20. The game move is e4, which the engine rates well below its first choices.

line.say: White plays e4, a move the engine rates well below its first choices.

claims.statement: 20.e4 is legal.
At depth 16 the engine rates 20.e4 at least 150 centipawns below its first choice.

steps.caption: After 20...fxe4. Step through the next exchanges.

line.say: Black lets the knight on h5 be taken.
The queen takes the knight.
The rook takes the pawn on f2.
The queen goes to g5.
The second rook joins on the f-file. The engine at depth 16 prefers h6 here by a small margin.
The king steps to h1. Black to move.

claims.statement: 20...fxe4 is legal.
At depth 16 the engine rates the position before 20...fxe4 as better for Black by at least 2 pawns.

steps.caption: After 23...R8f5 White's queen has to move. Then it is your turn again.

line.say: The rook attacks the queen on g5.
The queen goes to e3. Black to move.

claims.statement: 23...R8f5 is legal.
At depth 16 the engine rates the position before 23...R8f5 as better for Black by at least 3 pawns.

steps.caption: The game move was 24...Bd3. The engine's first choice at depth 16 is a different move, 24...Re2; close moves can change order with depth. Then White played Rce1.

line.say: The bishop reaches d3 and watches e2 and f1, squares White's rooks could use.
White's rook goes to e1. Black to move.

claims.statement: 24...Bd3 is legal.
At depth 16 the engine's first choice is Re2, not the game move.
After Bd3 two black pieces attack e2.
After Bd3 two black pieces attack f1.

steps.caption: 25...h6 was the last move of the game. Now test the position it leaves.

line.say: Black plays h6. White has 27 legal moves; the next steps test whether any of them avoids a loss.

claims.statement: 25...h6 is legal.

steps.prompt: Before reading on: suppose White could pass. Would passing be better or worse for White than the best real move? Write your guess.

steps.caption: The position after 25...h6, White to move. White has 27 legal moves.

claims.statement: White has exactly these 27 legal moves.
At depth 16 the engine rates the position, with White to move, as better for Black by between 5.3 and 6.2 pawns.
Kh2 is at least 200 centipawns below White's best move at depth 16.
g4 is at least 150 centipawns below White's best move at depth 16.
White's knight is still on b1, where it went at move 18.

steps.caption: The pass test: the same position with Black to move, as if White could pass.

claims.statement: At depth 16 the engine rates the position, with Black to move, as better for Black by between 6.4 and 7.2 pawns.

steps.text: **The pass test.** Zugzwang means every move is worse than passing. At depth 16 the engine rates the real position (White to move) about 5.5 to 6 pawns for Black, and the same position with Black to move about 6.5 to 7, roughly a pawn more. So White's best move is slightly better than a pass: White is lost, but by this test not in strict zugzwang, which fits the writers who dispute the name. Engine numbers are evidence, not proof.

steps.prompt: At which move do you think Black was already clearly ahead? Say why.

steps.text: **What decided it.** By the engine at depth 16, Black was at least two pawns ahead before 20...fxe4 and at least three before 23...R8f5, so the finish added to an existing lead. Core skills used: Zugzwang (the pass test), Pieces out of play (White's knight sat on b1 from move 18), Types of sacrifice (20...fxe4), The seventh rank (the rook on f2), Comparing resulting positions (each decision).

steps.prompt: Which of the four moments you played (17...b4, 20...fxe4, 23...R8f5, 25...h6) would you have missed in a game of your own? What would you have had to notice, or to test, to find it?
